title: Errors in a booking product
metaTitle: Errors a hurried guest can act on
excerpt: When a hurried guest hits a booking error, say what broke, whether the time is still held, and the one next tap. A code and a sad illustration waste the moment.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf, objects set out carefully that still need a label when one is wrong.
caption: The arrangement only works if you can tell what is missing. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a booking screen say when the time was just taken?
faqs.answer: Say that the specific time is gone, and show the next real times without making them re-enter their name. Keep whatever they already typed. Offer those next times in the same view. A sad illustration and a code do not help a guest who is standing on a pavement trying to finish.

faqs.question: Should a failed payment cancel the time?
faqs.answer: The screen has to say which of the two is true: the time is still held while they fix payment, or the time was released and they must pick again. Do not leave this implicit. A guest who is charged and also told the booking failed, or who is not charged and loses the only evening slot, will not sort it out from a toast.

faqs.question: Where should the error appear on a phone?
faqs.answer: Put it in the same view as the button they just tapped, above the keyboard if a field is the problem. The time they wanted should remain visible. A banner at the top of a long page is easy to miss when the thumb is at the bottom. A toast that vanishes is worse, because the explanation leaves and the confusion stays.

markdown:
Booking product error states are the screen a guest meets when the time, the card, or the connection fails. They are on a phone. They are in a hurry. Say what broke and what to do. A code and a sad illustration waste the moment they still had patience for.

The time they picked has to stay on screen. The name and contact they typed have to stay in the fields. The next tap has to be obvious with one thumb. If you clear the form and show a mascot, they will not rebuild the booking. They will text the business, or they will book someone else.

## Say which thing broke

Name the object. Tuesday at 9:00 is no longer open. The card was declined. The page lost its connection before the booking was saved. "Something went wrong" forces a hurried person to guess which of those it was, and the guesses have different remedies.

Say whether the time is still theirs. This is the sentence teams skip. Held while they retry. Released, so they need a new time. Already booked, so they should check their email instead of paying again. Those are three different products. One generic failure covers none of them.

Then one next action. Pick the next open time. Use another card. Try the save again. Do not offer a menu of Learn more, Contact, and Home as if they had leisure. Contact can be a quiet line under the action for when the one tap is not enough.

Use the same nouns as the happy path. If the button said Confirm Tuesday at 9:00, the error says Tuesday at 9:00 was not confirmed. "Reservation entity conflict" is the database speaking. The guest has a Tuesday, not an entity.

The W3C describes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a standard for content that is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A booking error has to meet that bar on a phone, in sunlight, with a thumb. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reminder that color, a vibrating phone, or a picture of a broken calendar is not the message. The words are the message.

## Keep what they already did

A hurried guest has already done the hard part: chosen a time and typed their details, often with one hand. Destroying that work is a second failure on top of the first.

Keep the selected service visible. Keep the time visible even if it is no longer available, so they recognize the screen as the continuation of their attempt. Keep the fields. If a single field is the problem, mark that field and leave the others alone.

If the time is gone, show the nearest alternatives under the sentence, already in their timezone. Do not send them back to a month view that has forgotten their name. The alternatives are the repair. The month view is a scenic route.

If the network failed and you are not sure the booking saved, say that. "We did not get a confirmation. Check your email before you try again, so you do not book twice." A double booking is worse than a pause. The pause needs a sentence. Guessing is how you charge someone twice and meet them angry.

Partial success needs a plain split. The time is held and the confirmation email failed. The time is booked and the calendar invite failed. Tell them which half is true and what you will do, or what they should do. "Success" with a missing invite, and no explanation, becomes a no-show you caused.

## The failures to write before you launch

You need sentences, not a set of custom illustrations. Write these before the first real guest, in the design file, next to the confirmation.

The slot was taken between tap and confirm. This will happen for popular times. The copy names the lost time and offers the next ones. Their details stay put.

Payment failed. Say whether the hold remains. Say that they were not charged, if that is true. If you cannot promise that yet, say you are checking, and do not show a green confirmation. A green check with a failed charge is how trust dies.

The card form rejected a field. Point at the field. "Check the expiry" is an action. "Invalid payload" is not.

There is no availability in the range they asked for. This is less an error than an answer, and it still needs a design. Name the next date that does have a time. Do not show an empty grid and a red toast.

They tapped Confirm twice. If the first tap worked, the second should show the existing booking, not create another and not scold them. Slow networks cause double taps. The interface should expect that.

The link is for a service you no longer offer. Say the service name they clicked, say it is not bookable, and show the closest public service if you have one. A bare 404 on a texted link looks like the business disappeared.

Keep the list short and real:

- Time taken, details kept, next times shown
- Payment failed, hold status said out loud, no false confirmation
- Field problem, that field marked, the rest kept
- Nothing open, the next real date named
- Double tap, one booking, a link to it
- Dead service link, a human explanation

If one of these cannot happen in your product, write "cannot happen" next to it so nobody adds a joke screen later.

## Put the message where the thumb is

The guest's eyes are on the button they just pressed, near the bottom of the phone. The message belongs there, or directly above that button. A banner at the top of a scrolled page is a message for a desktop window.

Do not rely on a toast. Toasts leave. Hurried people look up a second too late and find a form that looks untouched or, worse, emptied. An inline sentence stays until they act.

Do not take over the whole screen with an illustration unless there is truly no booking left to return to. Even then, the headline has to say what broke and the button has to do the repair. Go home is the wrong repair. Home is where they have to start the hunt again. Back to times is the repair.

A reference code for support can sit in small type under the sentence. It does not lead. The guest's job is to leave with a time, not to read your incident number aloud in a lobby.

Avoid jokes about clocks, calendars, and "time flying." They are in a hurry. Wit feels like you are not. Be specific and short. Tuesday at 9:00 is taken. The next time is Tuesday at 11:30.


## Timezone, hold, and the second tap

A hurried guest often meets a second failure that is really a misunderstanding. The time was shown in the studio's zone and they confirmed it in theirs. That is not a server fault, and it should not wear an error costume after the fact. The confirm step repeats the zone in the same sentence as the clock time. If they change the zone there, the held slot updates, or you tell them the hold was released. Do not keep a hold on a Pacific hour while the screen now reads as Eastern.

Double submission is the other ordinary case. The button felt dead, so they tapped again. If the first request is still in flight, the button stays busy and says it is sending. If the first request succeeded, the second tap opens the booking they already have. Creating two bookings and then showing an error about the duplicate is a problem the product caused. The copy can be proudly dull. One booking. Here it is.

Payment fields fail in ways that look like the calendar failed. Separate them. A declined card does not mean the chosen hour is gone, unless your hold policy says it does. Repeat that policy in the sentence. They should not have to remember a footnote from the previous screen while they are looking for another card on a bright pavement.
## Review it on a real phone, in a bad network

Book the last slot from another phone while you sit on the confirm step. Submit. You are checking that the lost time is named, the next time is one tap away, and the name field still has the name.

Turn on airplane mode and submit. You are checking that you do not show a confirmation you cannot prove, and that you do not clear the form.

Fail a test card. Read the screen at arm's length. If you cannot tell whether you were charged and whether the time is held, the copy is not done. Ask someone who did not build it to say those two facts back to you after one look.

Some of these "errors" are permissions. The guest can see a service and cannot book it. The time looks open and is staff-only. The next piece is [permissions in a booking product](/blog/permissions-in-a-booking-product). A rule that appears only as a failure after they filled the form is a rule you showed too late.

If you want those sentences designed with the booking flow, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). A confirmation screen is the easy frame. The taken slot, with the details still in the form, is the frame that decides whether the guest comes back.
